newsitem.title: SOMALIA: Italian minister in talks with Somali warlords.
newsitem.headline: Italian minister in talks with Somali warlords.

text.p: An Italian envoy met separately with two rival warlords in anarchic Somalia on Tuesday after failing to set up a joint meeting, clan officials said.

Minister of State for Foreign Affairs Rino Serri held talks first with north Mogadishu warlord Ali Mahdi Mohamed and later met south Mogadishu warlord Hussein Aideed. Both lay claim to the presidency.
Clan officials said Serri's efforts to hold a joint meeting with the rival warlords failed because of wrangles over representation and the agenda.

They said Ali Mahdi, who controls a larger network of Somali clans, had wanted the talks with Serri to address the issue of convening a national reconciliation conference. But Aideed had rejected the idea.
Serri said the international community had an obligation to help Somalia in the process of reconciliation and reconstruction.
"To this end Italy is ready and willing to do her part," Serri told reporters.

The Italian urged Somalis to seize the opportunity presented by Italy, Somalia's former colonial ruler, in working towards re-establishing Somalia as a unitary state to enable it to gain international recognition.

Somalia has been without central authority since 1991, when rebels overthrew late dictator Mohamed Siad Barre. But they soon turned their guns on each other in murderous battles that laid waste to the land and killed an estimated 30,000 people.
International efforts, including a huge U.S.-led United Nations peacekeeping mission, to restore law and order and revive Somalia as a unified state have failed.
Clan-based warlords reign across Somalia and in some places authority means lawless teenagers armed with automatic rifles.
On Monday, Serri told reporters in the Kenyan capital Nairobi that the international community was concerned Somalia was becoming a centre for political violence.
"It's been confirmed that so-called Afghan groups are in Somalia and it is possible the country could become and in some aspects has become a centre for terrorism," he said.
Serri declined to comment on an inquiry into alleged atrocities committed by Italians in Somalia during the United Nations peacekeeping mission.
